Clinical Reference

Traumatic Brain Injury (v2)

On this page
Traumatic brain injury is an alteration in brain function, or other evidence of brain pathology, caused by an external force. The impact itself is over before you arrive — everything you do is aimed at the secondary injury: keeping the brain perfused, oxygenated, normoglycemic, normothermic and decompressed while it heals.
Mild GCS 13–15 · Moderate 9–12 · Severe 3–8 Treat ICP above 22 mmHg · keep CPP 60–70 SBP floor 110 if age 15–49 or over 70; 100 if 50–69 Steroids increase mortality — CRASH-1, 25.7% vs 22.3% TXA within 3 h · 1 g over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 h
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Primary vs secondary injury — the only distinction that matters

Primary injury is the mechanical damage delivered at the instant of impact: cortex bruised against bone, bridging veins torn by acceleration, axons sheared where grey and white matter of different densities move past each other, the middle meningeal artery lacerated by a fracture line crossing it. By the time the patient reaches you, the primary injury is finished. Nothing in this guide changes it.

Secondary injury is everything that happens next — over minutes, hours and days — and it is the entire target of TBI care. It is not one process but a self-reinforcing loop of four: an excitotoxic cascade that kills neurons chemically, edema that adds volume, raised intracranial pressure that chokes off perfusion, and the ischemia that results, which releases more glutamate and restarts the cascade. Every drug, every ventilator setting, every osmotic bolus and every operation in this guide interrupts that loop at a specific point.

The cascade, step by step

Mechanical stretch depolarizes neuronal membranes and dumps glutamate into the synaptic cleft in quantities the astrocytic reuptake machinery cannot clear. Glutamate holds open NMDA and AMPA receptors — and because the cell is already depolarized, the magnesium block on NMDA is relieved, so the channels stay open rather than gating normally. Calcium floods in. That calcium overwhelms buffering, enters mitochondria, and triggers the mitochondrial permeability transition: ATP production collapses and reactive oxygen species pour out. Calcium simultaneously activates calpains and caspases, which digest the cytoskeleton from the inside. Without ATP, the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase stops, sodium and water follow into the cell, and you get cytotoxic edema — cells swelling behind an intact blood–brain barrier. In parallel, the barrier itself is physically torn, so plasma leaks into the interstitium as vasogenic edema. Both add volume to a container that cannot expand.

Layered on top: cortical spreading depolarizations — waves of near-complete loss of the transmembrane ion gradient that sweep across the cortex at 2–9 mm/min, recorded on electrocorticography in 55–90% of monitored severe TBI patients, peaking at days 1–2 and again at days 6–7. In already-injured tissue these waves trigger spreading ischemia: the normal hyperemic response inverts, and perfusion falls exactly where demand just spiked.

The secondary injury loop. Note the feedback arrow from ischemia back to glutamate release — this is why a single insult becomes a self-sustaining process, and why the whole of TBI management is about breaking the loop rather than treating any one box.

Monro–Kellie: why a fixed box changes everything

The adult cranium is a rigid container of roughly 1,500 mL holding three things: brain parenchyma (~80%), blood (~10%) and CSF (~10%). The Monro–Kellie doctrine states that because the total volume cannot change, any increase in one compartment must be matched by a decrease in another or the pressure rises. The brain's compensatory reserve is CSF displacement into the spinal subarachnoid space first, then venous blood displacement out of the cranium.

The consequence is that the pressure–volume relationship is exponential, not linear. Add 20 mL of hematoma to a brain with intact reserve and the ICP barely moves. Add the next 10 mL after the reserve is spent and the ICP doubles. This single curve explains the two most characteristic behaviours in TBI: the lucid interval of an expanding epidural hematoma, and the patient who is conversational at hour four and herniating at hour five.

The intracranial compliance curve. The same 10 mL of clot produces a trivial pressure change on the flat part and a lethal one past the knee — the patient does not deteriorate gradually, they fall off a cliff. ICP treatment threshold 22 mmHg per Brain Trauma Foundation 4th Edition (Level IIB).
a rigid suitcase packed exactly full. You can always cram one more shirt in at the start — you just compress the air out (that is CSF draining to the spinal canal, and venous blood being squeezed out). The zipper closes fine and the case looks normal from outside. But once every pocket of air is gone, the very next shirt is the one that splits the seam. Nothing about the earlier shirts warned you, because the case absorbed them silently. That is why "the patient was talking an hour ago" is never reassurance in head trauma — it just means they had reserve an hour ago.

Perfusion: CPP, autoregulation and why blood pressure is a brain drug

The brain is perfused by the gradient CPP = MAP − ICP. A normal brain defends its blood flow across a wide range of perfusion pressures by constricting and dilating arterioles — cerebral autoregulation. TBI frequently impairs or abolishes this, and a brain that has lost autoregulation is pressure-passive: flow simply follows pressure. Drop the MAP and the injured brain infarcts; raise it and cerebral blood volume rises, which raises ICP further.

This is quantifiable at the bedside with the pressure reactivity index (PRx) — the moving correlation between MAP and ICP. A negative PRx means autoregulation is intact (as MAP rises, vessels constrict, cerebral blood volume and ICP fall). A PRx above roughly 0.25–0.3 means it is lost (as MAP rises, vessels dilate passively and ICP rises with it) and is associated with worse outcome and higher mortality. It is also the basis for individualized "CPPopt" targeting instead of a single number for every patient.

Autoregulation. The green plateau is why a healthy person tolerates a wide blood-pressure range without brain injury. The red dashed line is the injured brain: no plateau, so both hypotension and hypertension are directly harmful, and the safe window collapses to a narrow band you must actively defend.
A single episode of hypotension in severe TBI is one of the most powerful modifiable predictors of poor outcome — which is why the Brain Trauma Foundation sets an age-stratified floor rather than a range: SBP ≥110 mmHg if 15–49 or over 70 years, ≥100 mmHg if 50–69. Note the counter-intuitive shape: the youngest and the oldest patients need the higher floor.

Herniation — the anatomy of dying from pressure

When compensatory reserve is exhausted, tissue moves along the path of least resistance across the fixed dural and bony partitions. Each route compresses a predictable structure, so each has a signature you can read at the bedside without imaging.

SyndromeWhat moves whereBedside signature
Uncal (lateral transtentorial)Medial temporal lobe (uncus) over the tentorial edge onto CN III and the cerebral peduncleIpsilateral dilated, sluggish then fixed pupil (parasympathetic fibres run on the outside of CN III, so they go first) → contralateral hemiparesis → declining consciousness. A Kernohan's notch phenomenon can put the weakness ipsilateral, falsely localizing.
Central (transtentorial)Diencephalon and midbrain forced downward through the tentorial notch by diffuse swelling or bilateral mass effectRostral-to-caudal deterioration: progressive obtundation → Cheyne–Stokes breathing → small reactive pupils becoming mid-position and fixed → decorticate then decerebrate posturing.
Subfalcine (cingulate)Cingulate gyrus under the falx cerebriOften silent early — this is what the "midline shift" measurement is capturing. Can compress the anterior cerebral artery → contralateral leg-predominant weakness.
TonsillarCerebellar tonsils down through the foramen magnum onto the medullaNeck stiffness, then abrupt apnea and cardiovascular collapse. Can obstruct CSF outflow and cause acute hydrocephalus.
Upward (ascending transtentorial)Posterior fossa mass pushes cerebellum up through the notchMidbrain distortion, CSF obstruction, compression of the superior cerebellar arteries → superior cerebellar infarction. Classically precipitated by draining an EVD too fast in a posterior fossa lesion.
Cushing triad — widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular respirations — is a late sign of critical intracranial hypertension. The mechanism explains the odd combination: brainstem ischemia triggers a sympathetic surge that raises blood pressure to restore perfusion; the carotid baroreceptors then sense that hypertension and fire a vagal reflex bradycardia; and the abnormal respiratory pattern reflects direct compression of brainstem respiratory centres. Hypertension with bradycardia in a head-injured patient is herniation until proven otherwise — do not "treat the blood pressure."

Why each therapy works — the through-line

Every intervention below maps to one specific step in the loop. If you can name the step, you can reason out the drug rather than memorizing it.

TherapyStep it interruptsMechanism
Hypertonic saline / mannitolBrain volumeCreate an osmotic gradient across a relatively intact blood–brain barrier and pull free water out of parenchyma into plasma. Reflection coefficient ~1.0 for hypertonic saline vs ~0.9 for mannitol — mannitol leaks slightly more. Mannitol adds a second, independent mechanism: it lowers blood viscosity, which improves oxygen delivery, which triggers autoregulatory vasoconstriction and shrinks cerebral blood volume.
CSF drainage (EVD)Monro–Kellie compartmentsPhysically removes the most compliant of the three compartments. An EVD does not treat the injury — it buys back the compensatory reserve the edema consumed, moving the patient back down the flat part of the curve.
Sedation / analgesiaMetabolic demandLowers CMRO₂; flow-metabolism coupling then reduces cerebral blood flow and blood volume. Also abolishes the ICP spikes caused by pain, coughing, suctioning and ventilator dyssynchrony.
HyperventilationCerebral blood volumeHypocapnia constricts cerebral arterioles within minutes. Bridge only — CSF pH re-equilibrates over hours so the effect fades, while the vasoconstriction can drop flow below the ischemic threshold in tissue that is already marginal.
Decompressive craniectomyThe container itselfRemoves the rigid boundary, converting a closed system into an open one so swelling displaces the scalp instead of the brainstem. It does not treat the swelling — it removes the penalty for swelling.
Barbiturate comaMetabolic demand (maximal)Pentobarbital suppresses energy-dependent synaptic transmission, cutting CMRO₂ by roughly half, with direct cerebral vasoconstriction on top. Reserved for refractory ICP; lowers the number reliably but has never been shown to improve outcome prophylactically.
Tranexamic acidOngoing bleedingBlocks plasminogen activation, so fibrin is not lysed and clot stabilizes. Purely hemostatic — it does nothing for edema or ICP, which is exactly why its benefit concentrates in patients who still have brain left to save.
Normothermia, glucose 140–180, Na 135–145, SpO₂ > 94%Every stepThe unglamorous half. Fever, hyperglycemia, hyponatremia and hypoxia each independently amplify the excitotoxic cascade and worsen edema. Most of the outcome benefit available on a ward is here, not in any drug.
Two therapies that seem mechanistically obvious and are actively harmful: corticosteroids (CRASH-1, n=10,008 — 6-month mortality 25.7% vs 22.3%, RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.07–1.24, p=0.0001) and therapeutic hypothermia (Eurotherm3235, POLAR and NABIS:H II all negative; Eurotherm stopped early for a harm signal). Both reliably do the physiological thing you want — steroids reduce vasogenic edema in tumours, hypothermia lowers ICP — and both kill people with TBI. Lowering the number is not the same as helping the patient.

Classification & severity

📊

Glasgow Coma Scale — the exact points

Teasdale and Jennett, Lancet 1974. Score each domain at its best response; the total runs 3–15. Report the components, not just the sum — E2V2M5 = 9 and E4V1M4 = 9 are the same number describing very different patients, and the motor score alone carries most of the prognostic weight.

PointsEye opening (E)Verbal (V)Motor (M)
6——Obeys commands
5—OrientedLocalizes to pain (moves purposefully toward the stimulus)
4SpontaneousConfused conversation — answers, but disorientedWithdraws from pain (normal flexion)
3To speech / verbal commandInappropriate wordsAbnormal flexion — decorticate
2To pain / pressureIncomprehensible soundsExtension — decerebrate
1NoneNoneNone
NTNot testable — e.g. eyes swollen shut, or intubated (score as "T", conventionally written 8T)

Severity bands

SeverityGCSWhat it implies operationally
Mild13–15~90% of all TBI. The question is whether to image, not whether to admit. Most go home.
Moderate9–12Always image, always admit, serial neuro checks, repeat CT. This is the group that "talks and deteriorates."
Severe3–8Cannot protect the airway by definition. Intubate, ICU, neurosurgery, consider ICP monitoring.
GCS-Pupils (GCS-P) = GCS − pupil reactivity score, where both reactive = 0, one unreactive = 1, both unreactive = 2 (Brennan, Murray & Teasdale, J Neurosurg 2018). It extends the scale to 1–15 and restores discrimination at the bottom end, where plain GCS 3 lumps together patients with very different survival. A GCS 3 with reactive pupils and a GCS 3 with both fixed are not the same conversation with the family.
Score the GCS after resuscitation, and document what is confounding it. Hypotension, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, alcohol, sedatives and paralytics all suppress the score without any additional brain injury — and a paralysed patient has no scoreable motor or verbal response at all. A GCS obtained during hypoxia and never repeated has misclassified more patients than any imaging error.
🧠

CT classification — Marshall and Rotterdam

Two systems, two purposes. Marshall (1991) is a categorical description of what the scan looks like and is what neurosurgeons speak. Rotterdam (Maas, Neurosurgery 2005) is an additive score built specifically to predict outcome, and is the one that goes into prognostic models.

Marshall CT classification

CategoryDefinition
Diffuse injury INo visible intracranial pathology on CT
Diffuse injury IICisterns present, midline shift 0–5 mm, no high- or mixed-density lesion >25 cm³ (may include bone fragments or foreign bodies)
Diffuse injury III (swelling)Cisterns compressed or absent, midline shift 0–5 mm, no high/mixed-density lesion >25 cm³
Diffuse injury IV (shift)Midline shift >5 mm, no high/mixed-density lesion >25 cm³
V — evacuated mass lesionAny lesion surgically evacuated
VI — non-evacuated mass lesionHigh/mixed-density lesion >25 cm³ not surgically evacuated
The two things Marshall is really asking you to look at are the basal cisterns and the midline. Compressed or absent cisterns mean the brainstem has run out of room around it and is the single most useful qualitative sign on a trauma head CT — more so than the size of any individual collection.

Rotterdam CT score

Rotterdam CT score calculator

Select all four components. A constant of +1 is added so the scale runs 1–6.
Two counter-intuitive quirks worth knowing. An epidural hematoma scores zero and its absence scores +1 — because an EDH is the one lesion that is often surgically curable, so its presence predicts a better outcome than the same mass effect from irreparable diffuse injury. And +1 is added to every total, purely so the scale reads 1–6 instead of 0–5.

Mortality figures from the original derivation (Maas AIR et al., Neurosurgery 2005;57:1173–82). Use them for calibration and counselling, not as an individual prediction — see the note on self-fulfilling prophecy in the ICU prognostication section.

Other scores, deliberately not reimplemented here: the Helsinki CT score (Raj 2014, range −3 to +14) and the IMPACT and CRASH prognostic models use continuous nomograms or regression equations whose exact coefficients could not be verified point-by-point for this build. Rather than guess the arithmetic, compute them at source: IMPACT (MDCalc) and the CRASH prognostic calculator (LSHTM).

🔬

The lesions — mechanism, CT signature, threshold

LesionVessel / mechanismCT signatureSurgical threshold
Epidural hematoma Arterial — middle meningeal artery lacerated by a temporal bone fracture crossing it Biconvex / lens-shaped, hyperdense. Does not cross suture lines (dura is fused to bone there) but does cross the falx and tentorium. Evacuate any EDH >30 cm³ regardless of GCS. Non-operative management is acceptable if <30 cm³, <15 mm thick, <5 mm shift, GCS >8, no focal deficit — with serial CT at a neurosurgical centre.
Acute subdural hematoma Venous — bridging veins torn by acceleration/deceleration; sometimes a cortical artery Crescentic, concave toward the brain. Crosses suture lines but is bounded by dural reflections, so it tracks along the falx (parafalcine) and tentorium. Evacuate if thickness >10 mm OR midline shift >5 mm, regardless of GCS.
Traumatic SAH Small pial/subarachnoid vessels, or extension from an adjacent contusion Hyperdensity in the convexity sulci — peripheral, not centred on the basal cisterns the way aneurysmal SAH is. Not itself surgical. It is a marker of injury severity and scores +1 on Rotterdam.
Cerebral contusion Brain striking bone — coup at the impact site, contrecoup opposite it; frontal and temporal poles are most exposed to rough bony surfaces "Salt-and-pepper" mixed hyper/hypodensity — petechial blood in edematous cortex. Blossoms over 24–48 h. Individualized on volume, location, mass effect and exam trajectory rather than a single number.
Diffuse axonal injury Rotational/angular acceleration shears axons where tissues of different density meet CT is often normal or near-normal — small petechial foci at grey–white junctions, corpus callosum, dorsolateral brainstem. SWI/GRE MRI is far more sensitive. None. Adams grading: I = grey–white junction; II = plus corpus callosum; III = plus brainstem.
Intraventricular hemorrhage Torn subependymal/choroidal veins, or reflux of subarachnoid blood Dependent hyperdensity layering in the occipital horns. EVD if it causes hydrocephalus. Scores +1 on Rotterdam.
The single highest-yield discriminator: epidural stops at sutures, subdural stops at dural reflections. So a collection that crosses the midline under the falx is not a subdural, and a collection that crosses the coronal suture is not an epidural. Shape is the shortcut (lens vs crescent), but when the shape is ambiguous — and in a thin early collection it often is — the boundary rule is the one that holds.
A normal first CT does not exclude significant TBI. Diffuse axonal injury is frequently CT-occult, and contusions blossom. A patient whose exam does not match their scan needs a repeat scan and an MRI — not reassurance.

Imaging atlas

🖼️

Read these six and you can read most trauma head CTs

Epidural hematoma. Left panel: a hyperdense biconvex collection over the right convexity (patient's right is on the image left), with a small associated intracerebral bleed. Right panel: the same study in bone window, showing the calvarial fracture. Always look at bone windows — the fracture tells you which vessel was torn and predicts where the collection will grow.
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons: Epidurale Blutung - CT - WT-KF.jpg
Subdural hematoma — parafalcine. 74-year-old after a fall. Hyperdense blood layered along the falx on all three planes, with bilateral convexity subarachnoid blood. This is the boundary rule made visible: subdural blood is not confined by sutures, so it spreads along dural reflections instead of forming the lens shape of an epidural.
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons: Parafalzines Subduralhaematom 74M - CT - 001.jpg
Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage. Hyperdense blood filling the convexity sulci on the left. Contrast this distribution with aneurysmal SAH, which centres on the basal cisterns and interhemispheric fissure — traumatic SAH is peripheral because the bleeding is from small surface vessels sheared at the site of impact.
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons: Subarachnoidalblutung traumatisch 83W - CT - 001.jpg
Contusions, and what CT misses. 54-year-old with TBI. A: admission CT — bifrontal contusions with right frontotemporal subarachnoid blood. B: follow-up CT, largely resolved. C and D: susceptibility-weighted MRI of the same brain, where arrowheads mark numerous hemosiderin-laden microhemorrhages that were never visible on either CT. This is the single best argument for MRI when the exam is worse than the scan.
Zhao H, Wang J, Lu Z, Wu Q, Lv H, Liu H, Gong X — CC BY 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons: CT and MRI of cerebral hemorrhages…
Diffuse axonal injury — and the blossoming lesion. Motorcyclist. Left: CT immediately after the crash, showing only a tiny hyperdensity adjacent to the corpus callosum (circled). Right: the same slice at 6 hours — the lesion is clearly larger. Two lessons in one image: DAI hides at the corpus callosum and grey–white junctions, and an early CT is a snapshot of a moving process, not a verdict.
Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons: Diffuse axonal injury-CCT Unfallaufnahme und nach 6h.jpg
Measuring midline shift. Draw a line between the anterior and posterior falx attachments, then measure perpendicular from that line to the septum pellucidum. Here a left frontal extra-axial mass has effaced the left lateral ventricle and pushed the midline right, with surrounding white-matter edema. >5 mm is the threshold that drives both Marshall class IV and the Rotterdam midline point. Note: this teaching case is a non-traumatic extra-axial lesion — the measurement technique and the mass-effect findings are identical in trauma.
Cerevisae, CC BY-SA 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons: Left frontal extra-axial lesion causing vasogenic odema and midline shift…
Anisocoria — the exam finding that outranks the scan. A new unilateral dilated, sluggish pupil in a head-injured patient is uncal herniation compressing CN III until proven otherwise, and it mandates immediate hyperosmolar therapy, neurosurgical notification and a repeat CT — in that order, not after imaging. Pupil reactivity is also one of only three variables in the IMPACT core prognostic model. This teaching image shows anisocoria from a non-traumatic cause; what matters is recognizing the asymmetry itself.
Russavia, CC BY 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons: Anisocoria.jpg

How it presents

🔍

Symptoms and signs — frequency and mechanism

Frequencies vary widely by cohort and by how soon after injury you ask, which is itself informative: figures from acute-care cohorts (people who sought help) run much higher than population samples. Both are given below where available.

Symptom / sign~FrequencyWhy it happens
Headache55% general cohort
92% acute-care cohort		Trigeminovascular activation and irritation of dural/meningeal nociceptors — the brain has no pain fibres, the meninges do. Compounded by the metabolic mismatch of the excitotoxic cascade.
Photophobia74% of those with post-traumatic headacheTrigeminal sensitization plus thalamocortical hyperexcitability — the same central sensitization that drives migraine photophobia.
Phonophobia72% of those with post-traumatic headacheSame thalamocortical gating failure, in the auditory pathway.
Dizziness / imbalance41%Vestibular end-organ concussion, central vestibular (brainstem/cerebellar) dysfunction, and cervical proprioceptive disruption from the whiplash component. Worth separating — each responds to a different rehab.
Fatigue32%A genuine cellular energy crisis: mitochondrial dysfunction with increased demand from ionic pump restoration means the brain is running an energy deficit for days to weeks.
Nausea / vomiting26% general
55% with post-traumatic headache		Vestibular activation and area postrema stimulation. Repeated vomiting is different — it is a decision-rule criterion for imaging and can signal rising ICP.
Cognitive slowing23%Diffuse microstructural axonal injury degrades white-matter conduction; processing speed is the most sensitive casualty of losing conduction velocity.
Poor concentration21%Prefrontal and attentional network disruption — frontal poles sit against rough orbital bone and are among the most contusion-prone regions.
Memory difficulty21%Hippocampal and mesial temporal neurons are unusually rich in NMDA receptors, making them selectively vulnerable to the excitotoxic calcium load.
Sleep disturbance20%Disruption of hypothalamic and brainstem sleep–wake circuitry, with measurable melatonin dysregulation. Often the last symptom to resolve — and it amplifies every other one.
Amnesia (retro- or antegrade)Variable — a defining clinical signFailure of hippocampal encoding rather than a structural lesion. Duration of post-traumatic amnesia is a better severity marker than GCS in mild injury.
Loss of consciousness<10% of concussionsTransient disruption of the reticular activating system and thalamocortical arousal circuitry. LOC is neither necessary nor sufficient for concussion — most concussions have none.
Post-traumatic seizureUncommon in mild; higher with hemorrhageInjured cortex is hyperexcitable from glutamate excess and loss of inhibitory interneurons. An immediate impact seizure is not the same as epilepsy.

Moderate and severe presentation

LOC lasting minutes to hours, profound confusion or combativeness, slurred speech, inability to rouse from sleep, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizures, pupillary asymmetry or dilation, and clear fluid from the nose or ear (CSF leak from a basilar skull fracture).

Signs of intracranial hypertension or herniation that demand action before the next scan: a new asymmetric, dilated or non-reactive pupil; extensor (decerebrate) posturing; hypertension with bradycardia; or a GCS drop of ≥2 points. Any one of these means hyperosmolar therapy, airway control, and a neurosurgeon on the phone now.
Look for basilar skull fracture signs explicitly, because they change the decision rule: hemotympanum, "raccoon eyes" (periorbital ecchymosis), Battle's sign (retroauricular ecchymosis), and CSF oto- or rhinorrhea. Raccoon eyes and Battle's sign take hours to develop, so their absence early means nothing.
Workup

Who needs a scan

🧪

Decision rules, labs and biomarkers

Non-contrast head CT is the only imaging that matters acutely — it finds the blood you might have to operate on, and it is fast. MRI is more sensitive for DAI and microhemorrhage but is not an acute triage tool. The clinical question is never "would a scan show something," it is "would a scan change what I do in the next six hours."

Head-injury triage from door to disposition. The three GCS bands drive fundamentally different pathways — and note that the decision rules only apply in the mild band.

Canadian CT Head Rule

Applies to: minor head injury with GCS 13–15 within 24 h, and witnessed LOC, definite amnesia, or witnessed disorientation. Does not apply to patients on anticoagulants or with known coagulopathy, or those who seized after the injury — those patients get scanned regardless.

Canadian CT Head Rule

Tap every factor that is present.

High risk — for neurosurgical intervention
GCS <15 at 2 hours after injury
Suspected open or depressed skull fracture
Any sign of basilar skull fracture
Vomiting ≥2 episodes
Age ≥65 years
Medium risk — for clinically important brain injury
Amnesia before impact >30 minutes
Dangerous mechanism (pedestrian struck, ejected from vehicle, fall >3 feet or 5 stairs)
—
Select any criteria present, or none.

Performance (Stiell, Lancet 2001): high-risk criteria alone were 100% sensitive (95% CI 92–100%) for needing neurosurgical intervention while scanning only 32% of patients. Adding the medium-risk criteria gave 98.4% sensitivity (95% CI 96–99%) and 49.6% specificity for clinically important brain injury, at a 54% scan rate.

New Orleans Criteria

Applies to: minor head injury with GCS 15 specifically and witnessed LOC, definite amnesia, or witnessed disorientation. Any one criterion present means scan.

New Orleans Criteria

Headache
Vomiting
Age >60 years
Drug or alcohol intoxication
Persistent anterograde amnesia (short-term memory deficit)
Visible trauma above the clavicle
Seizure
—
Select any criteria present, or none.
Both rules are ~100% sensitive; they differ entirely in specificity. New Orleans includes headache and intoxication — near-universal in this population — so it scans almost everyone (specificity ~5–25%). The Canadian rule was built to cut imaging and does, which is why it is the default in most systems. Use New Orleans when you want the maximally conservative net in a GCS-15 patient, and remember neither rule was validated in anticoagulated patients.

Other instruments worth knowing

  • NEXUS Head CT: low-risk only if all eight are absent — skull fracture signs, scalp hematoma, neurologic deficit, abnormal alertness, abnormal behaviour, persistent vomiting, coagulopathy, age ≥65. Sensitivity 100% (95% CI 99.1–100) for neurosurgical intervention, specificity 24.9%.
  • PECARN (paediatric, not for adults): in children ≥2 y the predictors are severe mechanism, any LOC, any vomiting, severe headache, GCS <15, altered mental status, and basilar skull fracture signs; sensitivity 96.8% (100% in under-2s, where the criteria differ). Its purpose is to identify children safe to not scan.

Labs and blood biomarkers

CBC, CMP, coags (PT/INR, PTT)Any patient being admitted or with a positive scan. INR drives reversal decisions; platelets and creatinine drive drug choices.Baseline
Type and screenAny intracranial hemorrhage or planned operation.If bleed
Ethanol level, urine toxWhen intoxication is confounding the GCS. Documents why the exam is depressed so a later improvement is interpretable.If altered
GlucoseImmediately, in every altered patient. Hypoglycemia is the cheapest reversible cause of a low GCS.Immediate
GFAP + UCH-L1Adults ≥18 y, non-penetrating injury, GCS 13–15, sample within the validated window — to help rule out the need for CT. See below.Rule-out
CT cervical spineAny mechanism that could injure the neck; maintain precautions until cleared. The forces that injure the brain injure the c-spine.With head CT
CTA head and neckScreen for blunt cerebrovascular injury if modified Denver criteria are met — see the Wards order set.If criteria

GFAP and UCH-L1. Glial fibrillary acidic protein (astrocytic) and ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 (neuronal) leak into blood after injury. The Banyan Brain Trauma Indicator (FDA De Novo, February 2018) uses GFAP ≥22 pg/mL and/or UCH-L1 ≥327 pg/mL as positive, with the sample drawn within 12 hours of injury: sensitivity 97.6% and NPV 99.6% for a CT-visible lesion. The Abbott i-STAT TBI handheld platform (FDA 510(k), January 2021) uses different validated cutoffs — GFAP ≥30 pg/mL, UCH-L1 ≥360 pg/mL.

These are rule-out tests with a very high negative predictive value and a poor positive one — a positive result does not diagnose anything, it just fails to exclude. They are validated only in adults ≥18 y with GCS 13–15 and non-penetrating injury, within the time window, and they have not been validated inside the Canadian/New Orleans/NEXUS rules. Do not use them to override a decision rule that says scan.

S100B is the European equivalent: the Scandinavian Neurotrauma Committee guideline uses <0.10 µg/L as reassuring in its defined low-risk category — roughly 100% sensitivity, ~47% specificity, NPV >99%, cutting CT use by about 30% in eligible patients.
