Disposition from the ED

DispositionWhoConditions
DischargeIsolated mild TBI, negative CT (or no CT indicated by rule), GCS 15, no other injury needing admissionA sober, reliable observer at home, written return precautions, and a plan for follow-up. No observer means no discharge, regardless of the scan.
ED observation unitMinor positive imaging — e.g. a simple non-depressed skull fracture, or intracranial hemorrhage <5 mm in a fully conscious, neurologically intact patientSerial exams; repeat imaging if anything changes. In studied cohorts this is shorter and cheaper than admission with no excess risk.
AdmitAny GCS <15 persisting, any neurologic deficit, hemorrhage beyond minimal, anticoagulation with a positive scan, seizure, or no safe home situationSerial neuro checks; see the Wards panel.
The anticoagulated patient with a negative CT. Delayed intracranial hemorrhage after an initially negative scan occurs in roughly 1.8% on DOACs and 2.6% on vitamin K antagonists — and in the large multicentre series, none of those delayed bleeds required neurosurgical intervention. Routine admission, blanket 24-hour observation and protocolized repeat CT for every anticoagulated patient are therefore not well supported. Reserve repeat imaging for those who develop new symptoms, vomiting, or any clinical deterioration — and give unusually explicit return precautions to everyone else.
Return to the ED immediately for: worsening or severe headache, repeated forceful vomiting, increasing confusion or difficulty waking, seizure, new weakness or numbness, slurred speech, unequal pupils, clear fluid draining from the nose or ear, or worsening neck pain. Write these down and give them to the person who will be watching the patient, not just to the patient — a concussed person will not reliably remember a verbal list.
Treat

Concussion recovery

🏃

Return to learn and return to sport

The old advice — a dark room until symptoms stop — was wrong and made people worse. Concussion causes a transient energy crisis plus autonomic and vestibular dysregulation; prolonged inactivity deconditions the autonomic response, entrenches sleep disruption, and adds anxiety and social isolation on top. Sub-symptom-threshold aerobic exercise re-trains cerebral autoregulation and autonomic control without re-provoking the metabolic mismatch. That is why controlled exertion is treatment, not risk.

Relative rest for the first 24–48 hours only, then begin light activity that does not provoke symptoms. Strict prolonged rest is not supported and may prolong recovery.

Exercise tolerance can be quantified with the Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test: a modified Balke protocol starting at 3.2–3.6 mph with the incline increasing 1° per minute after the first minute, continued until symptoms increase by ≥2 points on the symptom scale, which defines the heart-rate threshold (HRt). Exercise is then prescribed at 80–90% of HRt, 20–30 minutes, 5 days a week. In Leddy's JAMA Pediatrics 2019 RCT of adolescents within 10 days of injury, subthreshold aerobic exercise shortened median recovery from 17 to 13 days versus stretching.

Graduated return to sport — the 6 steps (Amsterdam 2023 consensus)

1
Symptom-limited activity
Daily activities that do not provoke symptoms
▾

Gradually reintroduce normal daily activity — walking, light chores, screen time in tolerated increments. The goal is to re-engage life without spiking symptoms.

2
Light aerobic exercise
5–10 min walking, stationary bike or light jog
▾

Raise the heart rate at low intensity. This is where the sub-threshold prescription above lives.

3
Sport-specific exercise
Running, skating, drills — no head-impact risk
▾

Adds movement complexity and change of direction while keeping contact risk at zero.

4
Non-contact training drills
Harder training, may add resistance work
▾

Do not begin step 4 until the patient is back to baseline symptom score, with a normal exam and normal cognitive function, and has returned to full-time school or work. Steps 1–3 may be done while still mildly symptomatic; step 4 is the gate.

5
Full-contact practice
Requires medical clearance
▾

The first re-exposure to head-impact risk. Clearance is a clinician decision, not a coach or athlete decision.

6
Return to sport
Full competition
▾

Minimum 24 hours between steps. If symptoms increase by more than 2 points, stop, rest, and retry the previous step the next day.

Step structure per the 6th International Consensus Statement on Concussion in Sport (Amsterdam 2023), Br J Sports Med 2023;57:695–711, as summarized concordantly by CDC HEADS UP, the AAP and World Rugby. See the accuracy note in References regarding verbatim step wording.

Return to learn runs in parallel, and comes first. Students should go back to school as soon as tolerable, even part-time — early return is associated with better recovery than prolonged absence. Use accommodations (flexible attendance, rest breaks, reduced screen and testing load) to bridge the gap. A student must be back at school full-time before advancing past step 3 of return to sport.
Second impact syndrome — catastrophic diffuse cerebral swelling after a second head injury sustained before the first has resolved, attributed to loss of cerebrovascular autoregulation with hyperperfusion. It is rare (a few dozen well-documented cases since 1984) and its status as a distinct entity is debated, but ~95% of reported cases are under 18 and mortality exceeds 50%. It is the entire reason the return-to-sport ladder is not negotiable in adolescents.
What is and is not established — CTEChronic traumatic encephalopathy is a post-mortem neuropathological diagnosis. The defining lesion, per the Second NINDS/NIBIB consensus panel, is perivascular hyperphosphorylated tau in neurons in an irregular pattern at the depths of cortical sulci. There is no validated in-life diagnostic test, biomarker or imaging study, and individual-level causal attribution to any particular injury history is unproven. Counsel honestly: repetitive head impact exposure is a risk factor at the population level; nobody can tell a living patient whether they have CTE.
Treat

Persistent symptoms — drug ladders

💊

Post-traumatic headache, mood, sleep and agitation

Almost everything below is off-label for TBI specifically — these are migraine, depression and behavioural agents extrapolated into a TBI population. Two rules follow: start lower and titrate slower than you would otherwise (effective doses in TBI are often below general-population doses), and change one drug at a time so you can attribute both benefit and harm.

Post-traumatic headache prophylaxis

DrugStartTitrationTarget / maxWhy it worksMonitor / alternative
Amitriptyline10 mg at bedtime↑ by 10 mg every 1–2 weeksTarget 25–50 mg nightly; max ~100 mg/day Descending noradrenergic/serotonergic pain modulation; also treats the co-travelling insomnia and low mood Anticholinergic load, sedation, weight gain, QT. Lowers seizure threshold. Nortriptyline is the usual swap for better tolerability — no TBI-specific ladder is published, so titrate on the same schedule.
Propranolol40 mg twice dailyIncrease gradually as toleratedUsual effective 160–240 mg/day; max 240 mg/day. Stop if no response after 4–6 weeks at maximum Blunts the sympathetic/trigeminovascular drive; the same β-blockade also helps post-traumatic agitation and autonomic storming Bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue, masked hypoglycemia. Avoid in asthma and decompensated heart failure. Alternative β-blocker: metoprolol.
TopiramateWeek 1: 25 mg each eveningWeek 2: 25 mg AM + 25 mg PM · Week 3: 25 AM + 50 PM · Week 4: 50 AM + 50 PMTarget 100 mg/day (50 mg twice daily) Multiple: sodium-channel blockade, AMPA/kainate antagonism, enhanced GABA — dampens the cortical hyperexcitability that drives both headache and seizure risk Use judiciously in TBI — cognitive slowing and word-finding difficulty are its signature side effects and are indistinguishable from the injury you are treating. Also paresthesias, weight loss, renal stones, metabolic acidosis. Slow the titration if the patient is already cognitively symptomatic.
Gabapentin300 mg at nightTitrate weeklyStudied up to 2,400 mg/day divided α2δ calcium-channel subunit binding reduces excitatory neurotransmitter release Weak evidence — pooled RCT data did not show significant benefit over placebo for headache prophylaxis. Reasonable when there is coexisting neuropathic pain or autonomic storming; not a first choice for headache alone. Renally dosed.
Medication-overuse headache will silently undo all of the above. ICHD-3 thresholds: ≥10 days/month for triptans, ergots, opioids and combination analgesics (or for any mixture of classes); ≥15 days/month for simple analgesics and NSAIDs — each for more than 3 months. Ask about abortive frequency at every visit, and count over-the-counter use.

Mood, sleep and behaviour

DrugStartTitrationTarget / maxWhy it worksMonitor / alternative
Sertraline25–50 mg daily (use 25 mg if anxious or frail)↑ 25–50 mg every 1–2 weeks, minimum 1 week per step50–200 mg/day; max 200 mg SSRI — the best-tolerated antidepressant class post-TBI, with minimal anticholinergic burden and little effect on seizure threshold GI upset, hyponatremia (check sodium — this population is already prone to SIADH), sexual dysfunction. Response by ~2 weeks, maximal by 12. Alternatives: escitalopram; avoid highly anticholinergic agents such as paroxetine.
Melatonin (prolonged-release)2 mg, 2 hours before bedtimeFixed dose; reassess at 4 weeks2 mg nightly Restores the disrupted circadian signal directly, without sedating the cortex or impairing memory consolidation Essentially benign. This is the correct first-line hypnotic in TBI. RCT evidence in TBI patients supports the 2 mg prolonged-release, 4-week course.
Trazodone25–50 mg at bedtime↑ slowly as neededCommonly up to ~100 mg at bedtime (off-label) 5-HT2 antagonism plus antihistamine effect produces sleep without GABA-A agonism Orthostasis, next-day grogginess, rare priapism. Reasonable second-line, especially with comorbid depression. TBI-specific dosing evidence is weak — see the accuracy note in References.
Amantadine100 mg twice dailyTitrate as tolerated within the studied range200–400 mg/day total NMDA antagonism plus indirect dopaminergic agonism — targets the frontal dopaminergic hypofunction behind post-TBI apathy, inattention and slowed arousal Insomnia (dose early), livedo reticularis, hallucinations, lowers seizure threshold. Renally cleared — reduce in CKD. Giacino's NEJM 2012 trial showed it accelerates the pace of recovery during treatment; the benefit attenuates after stopping.
Propranolol (agitation)10 mg three times daily, or 20 mg every 6 hoursIncrease as tolerated by heart rate and blood pressureCase-reported titration to 160 mg daily long-acting; ward practice 20–60 mg every 4–6 h Blocks the peripheral and central sympathetic overdrive of post-traumatic agitation and autonomic storming — it is the agent with the best evidence base for TBI agitation Dose it standing, not as needed — it reduces the intensity of agitation, not its frequency, so PRN dosing chases the episode instead of preventing it.
MethylphenidateStart low, titrate slowly—— Dopaminergic/noradrenergic reuptake blockade; improves processing speed and inattention in RCTs, with associated reduction in anger and improved psychosocial function No TBI-specific dose ladder could be verified for this build — dose from a general stimulant reference and remember effective TBI doses are often lower than in ADHD. Monitor heart rate, blood pressure, appetite and sleep.
Drugs to avoid or use with real caution after TBI
• Benzodiazepines — associated with impaired long-term motor and cognitive recovery and prolonged post-traumatic amnesia. Not for routine agitation or sleep.
• Zolpidem and other "Z-drugs" — same recovery concerns; melatonin first, trazodone second.
• First-generation antipsychotics, especially haloperidol — D2 blockade opposes the dopaminergic recovery the frontal lobes are attempting, with animal and retrospective human data suggesting impaired recovery, plus QT prolongation, extrapyramidal effects and a lowered seizure threshold. If an antipsychotic is genuinely required, use a second-generation agent at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time.
• Valproate, risperidone, olanzapine and carbamazepine for agitation — newer studies failed to show efficacy versus control.
• Topiramate — effective for headache but cognitively costly in exactly the population least able to afford it.
• Anticholinergics generally — additive to the injury's own attentional and memory deficits.
Monitor

Follow-up cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

WhenWhatWhy
24–72 h after ED dischargePhone or in-person check: symptom trajectory, whether the observer noticed anything, adherence to relative restCatches the delayed bleed and the patient who was discharged into an unsafe situation.
1–2 weeksSymptom inventory, begin graded exertion, screen for headache pattern and sleepMost concussions are recovering by now. Ones that are not need a plan, not more rest.
4 weeks and beyondPersisting symptoms → targeted referral: vestibular/oculomotor therapy, cervical physiotherapy, neuropsychology, headache clinicPersistent symptoms are usually a treatable subtype, not an untreatable injury. Sort them into vestibular, cervicogenic, headache, mood, sleep and cognitive buckets and treat each.
Starting a new agentRecheck in 2 weeks; sodium with any SSRI; heart rate and blood pressure with propranolol; cognition with topiramateTitration only works if someone measures the response.
3 months after moderate–severe TBIAnterior pituitary screen — morning cortisol, TSH/free T4, LH/FSH, testosterone or estradiol, prolactin, IGF-1About 56% have at least one impaired axis at 3 months. It presents as fatigue, low mood and poor recovery — and gets blamed on the brain injury.
Post-traumatic epilepsy risk stratification matters for driving and work counselling: seizures are classed as immediate (<24 h), early (24 h–7 days) and late (>7 days) — only late seizures define post-traumatic epilepsy. Incidence is under 1–10% in mild TBI and roughly 6–12% in moderate, rising with intracranial hemorrhage, contusion, subdural hematoma, midline shift, and early seizures. Driving restrictions after a seizure are set by state law (commonly a 6-month seizure-free interval, but jurisdiction-dependent) — check the local DMV rule rather than quoting a number.
Modify

Comorbidity interactions

🔗

How the usual comorbidities change this disease

ComorbidityEffect on the injuryEffect on your management
Anticoagulation (warfarin, DOAC)Hemorrhagic progression; worse functional outcome in several analyses. Delayed bleed after a negative CT ~2.6% on VKA, ~1.8% on DOAC.Scan regardless of decision rules. Reverse immediately if there is any bleed (see Wards). Do not reflexively admit and rescan a well patient with a negative CT — target repeat imaging at new symptoms.
Antiplatelet therapySimilar concern for progression; qualifies the patient for BIG-3 tier regardless of lesion size.Do not transfuse platelets empirically — the PATCH trial showed harm (adjusted OR 2.05 for death or dependence). Reserve for pre-operative correction per local neurosurgical protocol.
Alcohol use disorderConfounds the GCS both ways; independently causes coagulopathy through hepatic synthetic failure; strongly predicts recurrent TBI.Intoxication is itself a New Orleans criterion. Document the ethanol level so a later GCS improvement is interpretable. Anticipate withdrawal on the ward — and remember benzodiazepine treatment of withdrawal conflicts with avoiding benzodiazepines after TBI, so use symptom-triggered dosing and taper deliberately.
Cirrhosis / coagulopathyImpaired factor synthesis and thrombocytopenia compound the TBI-induced coagulopathy that already occurs in ~33–35% of patients independent of any drug.Lower threshold to check and correct coagulation studies, and to repeat the scan. Expect the INR to under-represent the true bleeding risk.
Older age (>65–75)Bridging veins are stretched by atrophy, so subdurals form after trivial mechanisms; outcomes are substantially worse; frailty and polypharmacy compound.Age ≥65 is itself a scan criterion in both the Canadian rule and NEXUS (>60 in New Orleans). Apply the higher BP floor (SBP ≥110 for >70 y). Address falls prevention before discharge — this is a sentinel event.
Dementia / baseline cognitive impairmentRaises fall risk (feeding back into TBI risk) and makes "altered mental status" nearly impossible to interpret without a collateral history.Get a baseline from a caregiver before deciding anything. Have a lower threshold for imaging and for admission when no reliable observer exists.
Pre-existing epilepsyAdditively lowers seizure threshold with the injury itself.Continue home anti-seizure medication; do not simply layer prophylactic levetiracetam on top without reconciling the regimen. Driving restrictions stack.
Prior TBICumulative cognitive effects; in the acute window, the risk that motivates the return-to-sport ladder.Be conservative with clearance timing. Take a deliberate history of previous concussions — patients rarely volunteer them.
CKDNot a direct injury modifier.Affects drug dosing throughout — levetiracetam, gabapentin and amantadine are all renally cleared, and mannitol needs a functioning kidney to work and to be excreted. Weigh contrast risk if CTA is being considered.
Obstructive sleep apneaNocturnal hypoxemia is a secondary insult delivered every night during recovery.Continue home CPAP unless there is a basilar skull fracture or CSF leak, where positive airway pressure risks pneumocephalus — clear it with neurosurgery first.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & prevention

🛡️

The visit after the injury is a prevention visit

GradeRecommendationPopulationRelevance to TBI
BExercise interventions to prevent falls (2024)Community-dwelling adults ≥65 y at increased fall riskFalls are the leading mechanism of TBI in older adults. A geriatric head injury is the increased-risk criterion — this is the single most actionable prevention item on the list.
BScreening for unhealthy alcohol use with brief behavioural counselling (2018)Adults ≥18 y, including pregnant personsAlcohol is both a major TBI risk factor and a driver of recurrence. The ED or follow-up visit is a teachable moment with genuine evidence behind it.
BScreening for depression and suicide risk (2023)All adultsDepression is one of the commonest post-TBI sequelae and is treatable; it also masquerades as "persistent post-concussive symptoms."
BScreening for intimate partner violenceWomen of reproductive ageIPV is a substantially under-recognized TBI mechanism. Repeated head injury with an inconsistent or evolving history should prompt a private, direct screen.
CMultifactorial fall-prevention interventions (2024)Community-dwelling adults ≥65 yGrade C — offer selectively based on individual circumstances rather than universally.

Beyond USPSTF: review and deprescribe fall-risk medications (sedatives, antihypertensives causing orthostasis, anticholinergics); check vision; assess home hazards; consider vitamin D and bone health where a fragility fracture accompanies the head injury; and reinforce helmet and seatbelt use for the mechanism that actually injured this patient.

Escalate

When to send to the ED

🚑

From clinic to emergency care

Send now, by ambulance: GCS below 15 that is not improving, or any drop of ≥2 points · new focal deficit · new pupillary asymmetry · seizure · repeated vomiting · severe or escalating headache · suspected basilar skull fracture (hemotympanum, raccoon eyes, Battle's sign, CSF leak) · any head injury on an anticoagulant that has not yet been imaged · suspected non-accidental injury.
Refer, but not emergently: symptoms persisting beyond 4 weeks despite a graded activity plan → concussion clinic or neurology · isolated dizziness or visual tracking difficulty → vestibular and oculomotor therapy · neck-dominant symptoms → cervical physiotherapy · cognitive complaints affecting work or school → neuropsychology · a first late (>7 day) seizure → neurology for post-traumatic epilepsy management and driving counselling · fatigue with low mood after moderate–severe TBI → endocrine screen before assuming it is depression.
🛏️ Wards — the patient with a bleed who is not (yet) in the unit
Admit

Who to admit, and where

📋

Admission criteria and bed level

LevelCriteria
Floor / telemetrySmall stable intracranial hemorrhage with GCS 15, no midline shift or swelling on the initial CT, isolated head injury, age under ~55–65, not anticoagulated, and a normal exam.
Step-down / intermediateAny of: age >55, GCS 13–14, pre-injury warfarin or DOAC, hemorrhage that is more than minimal, or a mechanism/comorbidity profile that makes deterioration plausible. These three factors — GCS <15, age >55, pre-injury warfarin — are the ones independently associated with neurologic decline.
ICUSevere TBI (GCS ≤8 after resuscitation), need for airway protection or ventilation, need for ICP monitoring, hemodynamic instability, post-operative, or any moderate TBI with clinical or radiographic deterioration.
"Talk and deteriorate" is a real and quantified phenomenon. Among patients presenting with GCS 13–15 and an abnormal CT, meta-analysis found clinical deterioration in 11.7%, neurosurgical intervention in 3.5%, and death in 1.4%. A normal conversation does not mean a safe trajectory — it means they are still on the flat part of the compliance curve.

Brain Injury Guidelines (BIG) tiers

The BIG framework (Joseph, J Trauma Acute Care Surg 2014) stratifies TBI with intracranial hemorrhage by neurologic exam, intoxication, antithrombotic use and CT findings, to identify who genuinely needs neurosurgical consultation and repeat imaging.

TierProfileManagement
BIG-1Normal neurologic exam, no intoxication, no anticoagulant or antiplatelet, no or minimal skull fracture, smallest-volume findings, no intraventricular hemorrhage, no midline shiftObserve ~6 hours. No repeat CT, no neurosurgical consult. In the derivation cohort no BIG-1 patient deteriorated clinically or radiographically or needed intervention.
BIG-2Normal neurologic exam, may be intoxicated, not on antithrombotics, intermediate imaging findingsAdmit for observation. Repeat CT and neurosurgical consultation not routinely required. Radiographic worsening occurred in 2.6%.
BIG-3Abnormal neurologic exam, and/or any anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, and/or larger lesion burden or displaced fractureHospitalize, neurosurgery consult, repeat CT. Every patient in the cohort who required neurosurgical intervention (13% overall) was BIG-3.
Accuracy noteThe BIG tiers are presented here at the categorical and management level, which is what was verifiable. Published secondary sources describe millimetre thresholds for each hematoma type (broadly ≤4 mm, 5–7 mm and ≥8 mm across the three tiers) but the primary-source table could not be confirmed cell-by-cell for this build. Use your institution's adopted BIG or mBIG protocol for the exact millimetre cutoffs rather than the numbers in this paragraph.
Orders

Admission order set

🧪

Labs, imaging, monitoring and physiologic targets

Neuro checksq1h for the first 24 h in anyone with a bleed, GCS <15, or on antithrombotics; q2h once stable and low-risk. Specify GCS components and pupils, and give the nurse an explicit call-parameter: "call for GCS drop ≥2, new pupil asymmetry, or new deficit."Admit
HOB 30 degreesHead midline, no tight cervical collar ties, no hip flexion. Free jugular venous outflow is a no-cost ICP intervention that is undone constantly by repositioning and collars.Continuous
C-spine precautionsUntil cleared clinically and radiographically. The same force that injured the brain reached the neck.Until cleared
CBC, CMP, PT/INR, PTTOn admission and daily while there is an active bleed or antithrombotic reversal. TBI itself induces coagulopathy in about a third of patients independent of drugs.Admit + daily
Type and screenAny intracranial hemorrhage, any candidate for operation.Admit
Ethanol, urine toxicologyWhen intoxication confounds the exam — it documents why the GCS is low and predicts withdrawal.If altered
ABGSevere TBI or any respiratory compromise. You need the PaCO₂, not just the SpO₂ — end-tidal CO₂ is not a reliable substitute in trauma.If severe
Repeat head CTTriggered, not routine. Scan for a GCS drop ≥2, new pupillary asymmetry, new deficit, or new signs of raised ICP — the yield rises to ~40% in that setting. Routine scheduled repeat scans show radiographic progression in 20–35% but change management in <1%. Do repeat if coagulopathic or after reversal.If change
CT cervical spineWith the head CT for any concerning mechanism.Admit
CTA head and neck (BCVI screen)Modified Denver criteria — see below. Missed blunt cerebrovascular injury presents as a stroke days later in a patient who was improving.If criteria
DietNPO if depressed consciousness or a possible operation; otherwise diet with aspiration precautions and a swallow screen. Start nutrition early — see below.Admit
Glucose target 140–180 mg/dLDo not use tight control — targeting 81–108 mg/dL was associated with increased mortality in TBI meta-analysis. Hypoglycemia in an injured brain is a second injury.Continuous
Temperature 36.0–37.5 °CControlled normothermia — treat fever aggressively with acetaminophen and cooling. Do not induce hypothermia.Continuous
Sodium 135–145 mEq/LCheck at least daily. Hyponatremia expands brain water and drops the seizure threshold; it is common here and has two opposite causes (see complications).Daily
Blood pressure floorSBP ≥110 mmHg if age 15–49 or over 70; ≥100 mmHg if age 50–69. Write it as a floor with a call parameter, not as a range.Continuous
SpO₂ > 94%Hypoxia is an independent predictor of poor outcome. Supplemental oxygen, and escalate early rather than watching a drift.Continuous
The BP floor is age-stratified because the underlying data showed different mortality inflection points by age group, not because older patients tolerate less. Note the shape is not monotonic: the 15–49 and >70 groups both need SBP ≥110, while the 50–69 group's threshold is ≥100. Most people misremember this as "higher with age" — it is not.

Blunt cerebrovascular injury screening — modified Denver criteria

Scan immediately (signs already present): arterial hemorrhage from the neck, nose or mouth · cervical bruit in a patient under 50 · expanding cervical hematoma · focal neurologic deficit unexplained by the brain imaging (Horner syndrome, TIA, hemiparesis, vertebrobasilar symptoms) · stroke on CT or MRI.

Screen on mechanism plus associated injury: Le Fort II or III facial fracture · mandibular fracture · complex skull-base or occipital condyle fracture · any cervical spine fracture, subluxation or ligamentous injury · severe TBI with GCS <6 · near-hanging with anoxic injury · clothesline or seatbelt neck injury with swelling · TBI with thoracic injury · scalp degloving · upper rib fracture · thoracic vascular or cardiac injury.

Treat

Acute management

💊

Stepwise inpatient therapy

1
Stop the bleeding and undo the anticoagulation
The only thing on this list with a clock attached
▾

Hematoma expansion is the single most modifiable acute threat. Reverse first and ask questions afterwards — you can restart an anticoagulant, you cannot un-herniate a brain.

Agent on boardReversalDoseWhy it worksCautions / alternative
Warfarin / VKA4-factor PCC (Kcentra) plus vitamin K INR 2 to <4 → 25 units/kg (max 2,500)
INR 4–6 → 35 units/kg (max 3,500)
INR >6 → 50 units/kg (max 5,000)
Vitamin K 10 mg IV alongside		 PCC replaces factors II, VII, IX and X within minutes. Vitamin K is slow but essential — without it the INR rebounds as the PCC clears. Thrombosis risk. FFP only if PCC is unavailable — it is slower, needs far more volume, and NCS/SCCM 2016 prefers PCC for VKA-associated intracranial hemorrhage at INR ≥1.4.
DabigatranIdarucizumab 5 g IV total, given as two 2.5 g boluses no more than 15 minutes apart A monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with ~350× the affinity of thrombin, stripping it off its target. In RE-VERSE AD a single 5 g dose was sufficient in 98% of patients. If unavailable, dabigatran is dialysable — a genuinely useful fact unique among the DOACs.
Apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxabanAndexanet alfa Low dose: 400 mg IV bolus at ~30 mg/min, then 4 mg/min infusion for 120 min (480 mg)
High dose: 800 mg IV bolus at ~30 mg/min, then 8 mg/min for 120 min (960 mg)
Low if apixaban ≤5 mg or rivaroxaban ≤10 mg and last dose ≥8 h ago; high if larger dose, any edoxaban, or timing unknown / <8 h		 A decoy factor Xa molecule — catalytically inactive but binds the inhibitor with high affinity, freeing native Xa. Not a free lunch. ANNEXA-I: hemostatic efficacy 67.0% vs 53.1% with usual care, but thrombotic events 10.3% vs 5.6%, including ischemic stroke. Where andexanet is unavailable, 4-factor PCC at ~50 units/kg is the common off-label alternative.
Aspirin, clopidogrel, ticagrelorUsually nothing Consider DDAVP 0.4 mcg/kg IV × 1. Platelets only for a planned neurosurgical procedure, per local protocol. DDAVP releases von Willebrand factor and factor VIII from endothelium, transiently improving platelet adhesion. Do not transfuse platelets empirically — PATCH found adjusted OR 2.05 (95% CI 1.18–3.56) for death or dependence with transfusion. DDAVP evidence is mixed: meta-analysis showed only a non-significant reduction in hematoma expansion and a signal toward worse neurologic outcome. Individualize.
Any TBI within 3 hTranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g IV over 8 hours Blocks plasminogen activation so formed clot is not lysed — purely hemostatic. CRASH-3: no significant effect overall (18.5% vs 19.8%), but a real reduction in head-injury death in the GCS 9–15 subgroup (5.8% vs 7.5%, RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.64–0.95). Give it early, and expect most benefit in patients who are not already devastated. Outside the 3-hour window the evidence does not support it.
2
Seizure prophylaxis — 7 days, then stop
One of the cleanest stop-dates in medicine
▾
Injured cortex is hyperexcitable from excess glutamate and loss of inhibitory interneurons. A seizure in this brain is a metabolic catastrophe — it spikes CMRO₂ and ICP exactly when supply is worst. Prophylaxis prevents early seizures; it does not prevent the development of epilepsy, because epileptogenesis is a different, slower process of network reorganization that these drugs do not touch.
DrugLoadMaintenanceWhy / evidenceMonitor
Levetiracetam (preferred)Commonly 20 mg/kg IV (rounded to the nearest 250 mg, max ~2,000 mg)1,000 mg IV/PO every 12 h × 7 days SV2A binding modulates synaptic vesicle release. Equivalent efficacy to phenytoin (early-seizure RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.64–1.88) with fewer adverse reactions — hence its displacement of phenytoin in practice. Irritability, agitation and mood change (relevant in an already-agitated TBI patient) — renally dosed. Note 500 mg twice daily left over half of neurocritical care patients subtherapeutic in one study; 1,000 mg twice daily performed better. Institutional loading protocols vary widely.
Phenytoin / fosphenytoin20 mg/kg IV (fosphenytoin: 20 mg PE/kg, max 1,500 mg PE, infusible faster and IM-capable)~5 mg/kg/day divided every 8 h, adjusted to level Sodium-channel blockade. The original evidence: Temkin, NEJM 1990 — early seizures 3.6% vs 14.2% with placebo (p<0.001), and no benefit for late seizures. That single trial is the whole basis for the 7-day rule. Hypotension and arrhythmia with fast infusion, purple glove syndrome, drug interactions, need for level monitoring and albumin correction. Reserve for levetiracetam intolerance or failure.
Stop at day 7. Continue only if the patient has had a clinical or electrographic seizure — and at that point you are no longer giving prophylaxis, you are treating post-traumatic epilepsy, which is a different indication with a different duration. Prophylaxis that quietly becomes a lifelong prescription is one of the commonest avoidable harms in this population.
3
VTE prophylaxis — the timing question
Two competing catastrophes, and a stable CT is the referee
▾

TBI patients are strongly prothrombotic and simultaneously bleeding into their heads. Start mechanical prophylaxis (sequential compression devices) on arrival in everyone. The question is when to add chemical prophylaxis, and the modified Berne–Norwood criteria answer it against a stable repeat CT:

RiskDefinitionStart chemoprophylaxis
LowSDH ≤8 mm, EDH ≤8 mm, contusion ≤20 mm diameter, single contusion per lobeAt 24 hours, after a stable repeat head CT
Moderate / highAnything exceeding those thresholds, or an ICP monitor in place, or post-craniotomyAt 72 hours, if the repeat CT is stable
DrugStandardWeight-based alternativeWhyNotes
Enoxaparin30 mg SC every 12 h50–59 kg → 30 mg BID · 60–99 kg → 40 mg BID · ≥100 kg → 50 mg BID, targeting anti-Xa 0.2–0.4 IU/mL Antithrombin-mediated factor Xa inhibition. Fixed low dosing leaves roughly 40% of trauma patients under-prophylaxed by anti-Xa. A weight-based, anti-Xa-targeted protocol in a 509-patient intracranial hemorrhage cohort had only 1.6% hemorrhage expansion. CrCl <30 → use unfractionated heparin instead.
Unfractionated heparin5,000 units SC every 8–12 h—Same pathway, shorter half-life. Preferred in renal failure or when you may need to reverse quickly (protamine works; it barely touches LMWH). Watch for HIT.
Do not reach for a prophylactic IVC filter. In a National Trauma Data Bank analysis, prophylactic IVC filtration on top of pharmacologic prophylaxis was associated with increased odds of both DVT and PE (OR 4.30 each) with no mortality benefit. Reserve filters for a documented VTE with a genuine absolute contraindication to anticoagulation. Note: no dedicated TBI trial compares enoxaparin 30 mg twice daily against 40 mg once daily — the literature compares fixed versus weight-based dosing instead.
4
Nutrition, agitation and the rest of the daily work
Where most of the actual outcome benefit lives
▾

Nutrition. Feed to attain basal caloric replacement by day 5, and no later than day 7 post-injury (BTF Level IIA, associated with decreased mortality). Transgastric jejunal feeding is recommended to reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia (Level IIB). TBI is a hypermetabolic, hypercatabolic state — starving these patients while awaiting a swallow evaluation is a real and common harm.

Agitation. First exclude the treatable causes, in this order: pain, a full bladder, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, infection, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, constipation, and new intracranial pathology. Then optimize environment — consistent staff, day/night lighting, family presence, minimal restraints. Only then reach for drugs.

DrugStartTitrationCeilingWhy / evidence
Propranolol20 mg PO every 6 h (or 10 mg three times daily)Increase as heart rate and blood pressure allow20–60 mg every 4–6 hBest evidence base of any agitation agent in TBI. Reduces the intensity of episodes, not their frequency — so it must be scheduled, not PRN.
Amantadine100 mg PO twice dailyAs tolerated within the studied range200–400 mg/dayRaises arousal and improves the pace of recovery (Giacino, NEJM 2012). Dose the second one early in the day — it causes insomnia. Renally cleared.
Dexmedetomidine0.2 mcg/kg/hr (skip the load to avoid hypotension)Titrate by 0.1–0.20.7 mcg/kg/hrα2 agonist — sedation without respiratory depression, and preserves an arousable, examinable patient. Watch bradycardia and hypotension.
Quetiapine12.5–25 mgTitrate slowlyLowest effective dose, shortest durationIf an antipsychotic is unavoidable, a second-generation agent is preferred over haloperidol. Monitor QT and sedation. Evidence for antipsychotics in TBI agitation is weak overall.
Avoid haloperidol (D2 blockade opposes dopaminergic recovery; QT; lowers seizure threshold), benzodiazepines (delirium, prolonged post-traumatic amnesia, impaired cognitive recovery) and physical restraints where avoidable — restraint frequently escalates agitation rather than containing it. Valproate, risperidone, olanzapine and carbamazepine failed to beat control for TBI agitation in newer studies; do not reach for them by reflex.
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend, and the complications to look for

Every day: GCS by component and pupils · sodium and serum osmolality · glucose · temperature · CBC and platelets · coagulation studies if anticoagulated or reversed · any seizure activity, clinical or electrographic · bowel and bladder · lines and devices out as soon as possible · mobilization and therapy engagement.

Hyponatremia: two opposite diseases with identical labs

Both SIADH and cerebral salt wasting produce a low serum sodium with a high urine sodium. Getting the distinction wrong is actively harmful, and the discriminator is volume status — nothing else reliably separates them.

SIADHCerebral salt wasting
Volume statusEuvolemic to mildly hypervolemicGenuinely hypovolemic — the whole disease
MechanismInappropriate ADH release → free water retention → dilutional hyponatremiaPrimary renal salt wasting (natriuretic peptide-mediated) → sodium and water lost → volume depletion with secondary ADH
CluesNormal or slightly high weight, no orthostasis, low-ish BUN/creatinine, normal uric acid response after correctionWeight loss, negative fluid balance, orthostasis, rising BUN/creatinine, high urine output
TreatmentFluid restrictionSodium and volume replacement — isotonic or hypertonic saline. Fludrocortisone can reduce the volume of hypertonic saline needed.
Consequence of getting it backwardsVolume overload — recoverableFluid-restricting a volume-depleted brain-injured patient worsens both the hypovolemia and the hyponatremia, and drops cerebral perfusion pressure. This is the dangerous error.

Other complications to anticipate

ComplicationRecognitionManagement
Central diabetes insipidusHigh urine output with dilute urine and rising sodium — the mirror image of the above. Suggests hypothalamic/pituitary stalk injury.Desmopressin, commonly 1–2 mcg IV (institutional ranges vary widely) or 10–20 mcg intranasally, plus free water replacement. Monitor sodium closely — DDAVP can drop it fast, and rapid sodium shifts have been associated with rising ICP in TBI.
Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivityEpisodic tachycardia, tachypnea, hypertension, hyperthermia, diaphoresis and posturing, often triggered by suctioning or turning. Scored with the PSH Assessment Measure: <8 unlikely, 8–16 possible, ≥17 probable.First-line: propranolol 20–60 mg every 4–6 h, gabapentin 300 mg three times daily titrating up (does not cause hypotension, so it combines well), baclofen. Second-line: clonidine 0.2–0.3 mg every 6 h, morphine for acute paroxysms, benzodiazepines only if necessary. Minimize triggers.
Post-traumatic hydrocephalusPlateauing or regressing recovery, gait change, incontinence, ventriculomegaly on imaging. Reported in 0.7–29% overall and 10–40% after decompressive craniectomy, though only ~1% of a large cohort needed a shunt.Neurosurgical assessment; shunt if symptomatic and the imaging fits.
CSF leakClear rhinorrhea or otorrhea after basilar skull fracture; "halo sign"; positional headache. Confirm with beta-2 transferrin.Head elevation, avoid nose-blowing, straining and positive-pressure ventilation via mask. Most close spontaneously; persistent leaks need neurosurgical or ENT repair. Prophylactic antibiotics are not routinely indicated.
Post-traumatic hypopituitarismFatigue, low mood, poor rehabilitation progress — attributed to the brain injury and missed. 56% have ≥1 impaired axis at 3 months (gonadotropic 32%, corticotropic 19%, somatotropic 9%, thyrotropic 8%).Check morning cortisol acutely if unstable. Formal anterior pituitary screen at ~3 months after moderate–severe TBI. Most recovery happens by 6 months.
Spasticity, heterotopic ossification, pressure injuryRising tone limiting function; a warm swollen joint with restricted range (HO risk is highest with severe TBI plus a long-bone fracture); skin breakdown over bony prominences.Early therapy, splinting and positioning; standard spasticity ladder (baclofen, tizanidine, botulinum toxin, serial casting); turning every 2 h and pressure-redistributing surfaces.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers

Transfer to ICU for any of:
• GCS drop of ≥2 points from the documented baseline, or any fall to GCS ≤8 (cannot protect the airway)
• New pupillary asymmetry or non-reactivity
• New focal neurologic deficit
• SBP below the age-stratified floor (<110 if 15–49 or >70 y; <100 if 50–69 y) despite fluids
• Any sign of herniation — Cushing triad, posturing, abrupt respiratory pattern change
• New or expanding hemorrhage, or new midline shift on repeat CT
• Any seizure, and especially status epilepticus
• Agitation requiring escalating sedation beyond what the floor can safely monitor
• Need for hyperosmolar therapy, an ICP monitor, or an operation
While you wait for the bed, in a herniating patient: head up 30°, head midline, loosen the collar · secure the airway if GCS ≤8 · hypertonic saline or mannitol now (3% NaCl 250 mL over 10–20 min, or 23.4% NaCl 30 mL over 10 min through a central line, or mannitol 1 g/kg) · ventilate to PaCO₂ 30–35 as a bridge only · call neurosurgery before the repeat CT, not after it. Do not treat the hypertension.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness and where they go next

Discharge readiness: neurologic exam stable or improving for ≥24 h · repeat imaging stable (or none indicated) · seizure prophylaxis course completed or a clear plan documented · anticoagulation decision made and written down, with an explicit restart date or a reason not to · pain and headache controlled on an oral regimen · nutrition adequate and swallow cleared · mobilizing safely or with a plan · a defined follow-up appointment and a caregiver who understands the return precautions.

Home

Independent in activities of daily living, cognitively safe, reliable support at home. Written concussion/TBI education and a follow-up date — not "call if worse."

Home health

Home is safe but needs skilled nursing, physical or occupational therapy visits. Good fit for the older patient with a small bleed and a new mobility deficit.

SNF

Needs 24-hour skilled nursing but cannot tolerate 3 hours of therapy per day, or lacks the rehabilitation potential/endurance for an IRF.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Can tolerate and benefit from 3 hours of therapy/day, 5 of 7 days (CMS "3-hour rule"; ~15 h over 7 days is an accepted equivalent), needs ≥2 therapy disciplines, and has rehabilitation potential. Brain injury is one of the 13 CMS "60% rule" qualifying diagnoses — TBI patients are exactly who IRFs exist for. Refer early; beds are the rate-limiting step.

LTAC

Medically complex and expected to need >25 days — prolonged ventilator weaning, tracheostomy with heavy secretions, complex wounds.

Hospice / palliative

Goals-of-care determined comfort focus. Involve palliative care early alongside active treatment, not only at the point of withdrawal — and see the prognostication caution in the ICU panel before framing any conversation around a predicted outcome.
Two scales you will see on rehab consults. The Disability Rating Scale is a ~30-point observer-rated instrument (0 = no disability to 29 = extreme vegetative state) covering arousal, cognitive ability for self-care, dependence and employability — it was built to track the whole arc from coma back to work. The Functional Independence Measure scores 18 items from 1 (total assistance) to 7 (complete independence), total 18–126; a total FIM below about 80 generally reflects a care burden that cannot be met at home.
Three things that get missed at discharge and cause readmission: (1) nobody documented the anticoagulation restart plan, so it is either never restarted or restarted blindly; (2) seizure prophylaxis was continued indefinitely because no stop date was written; (3) the driving conversation never happened. Put all three in the discharge summary explicitly.
🫀 ICU — defending perfusion against pressure
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

Severe TBI (GCS ≤8 after resuscitation) · need for airway protection or mechanical ventilation · need for ICP monitoring · hemodynamic instability or vasopressor requirement · immediately post-craniotomy or craniectomy · any moderate TBI with clinical or radiographic deterioration · refractory seizures · hyperosmolar therapy requirement.

"GCS ≤8, intubate" is a rule about airway protection, not about the brain. But in TBI it doubles as brain protection, because the hypoxia and hypercapnia of an unprotected airway are two of the most potent secondary insults there are. Intubate early, and use a technique that avoids both hypotension and an ICP surge — see the sedation section.
Monitor

Monitoring, access & targets

🩸

What to place, and what number to chase

ICP monitoring — who gets a bolt

Brain Trauma Foundation indications. Monitor ICP in all salvageable patients with severe TBI (GCS 3–8 after resuscitation) and an abnormal CT. Also monitor in severe TBI with a normal CT if ≥2 of three are present on admission: age >40 years · unilateral or bilateral motor posturing · SBP <90 mmHg.
DeviceAdvantageLimitation
External ventricular drainThe gold standard — it both measures pressure and treats it by draining CSF. Allows sampling and intrathecal therapy.Harder to place (needs a ventricle, which may be slit-like from swelling), and communicates with the ventricular system: in one large series 29.8% were started on empiric antibiotics for suspected infection with 4.1% culture-confirmed ventriculitis.
Intraparenchymal boltQuicker, easier, good waveform fidelity, lower infection risk.Cannot drain. Measures pressure locally, so it can under-read compartmentalized pressure. Drift over days.

Mortality is similar between devices in observational data (28.7% EVD vs 26.6% intraparenchymal at 30 days in one comparative series) — the choice is about whether you want a therapeutic option, not about survival.

The BEST-TRIP nuanceChesnut's NEJM 2012 trial (n=324, Bolivia and Ecuador) randomized severe TBI to ICP-monitor-guided care versus care guided by imaging and serial clinical examination. ICP-guided care was not superior (HR for death 1.10, 95% CI 0.77–1.57). This is routinely misquoted as "ICP monitoring does not work." What it actually showed is that a disciplined, protocolized algorithm — whether anchored to a number or to frequent scans and examinations — is what drives outcome. The monitor is a tool for executing the protocol, not a substitute for having one.

Brain tissue oxygen (PbtO₂)

BOOST-II (phase II) showed that adding PbtO₂ to ICP monitoring dramatically reduced the burden of brain tissue hypoxia — 74.9 vs 285.8 hours·mmHg (p<0.0001) — with a non-significant trend toward better outcomes, but it was never powered for efficacy. OXY-TC (Lancet Neurology 2023, 25 French centres) then found that ICP+PbtO₂-guided management did not reduce poor 6-month neurologic outcome, with more technical failures in the combined arm. The definitive phase III trial, BOOST-3, targets ICP <22 and PbtO₂ >20 versus ICP alone; its final results were not confirmed as published at the time of this build — check before quoting numbers.

Numeric targets

ParameterTargetBasis and the reason
ICPTreat above 22 mmHgBTF Level IIB. Raised from 20 to 22 based on threshold analysis. It is a trigger, not a goal — treat the sustained elevation and the trend, not a single transient spike from coughing.
CPP60–70 mmHgBTF Level IIB. Do not chase CPP above 70 with fluids and pressors — the aggressive-CPP strategy causes ARDS (Level III caution) without improving neurologic outcome.
PbtO₂> 20 mmHgBOOST-II / BOOST-3 protocol threshold. Detects tissue hypoxia occurring at an apparently acceptable ICP and CPP.
PaCO₂35–38 mmHg routineLow-normal. 32–35 as a tier-2 measure; 30–32 as tier-3 rescue only. Never prophylactically below 25 (BTF Level IIB), and avoid hyperventilation entirely in the first 24 hours when cerebral blood flow is at its lowest.
PaO₂ / SpO₂PaO₂ >100 mmHg · SpO₂ >94%Hypoxia is an independently powerful secondary insult. Avoid extreme hyperoxia too.
HemoglobinRestrictive — transfuse at ~7 g/dLHEMOTION (NEJM 2024, n=742): unfavourable GOS-E 68.4% liberal vs 73.5% restrictive, adjusted difference 5.4 points (95% CI −2.9 to 13.7) — not significant. Robertson (JAMA 2014) found more thromboembolic events with a Hgb 10 target. No proven benefit to liberal transfusion.
Glucose140–180 mg/dLTight control (81–108) was associated with increased mortality in TBI meta-analysis. Hypoglycemia in an energy-starved brain is a direct injury.
Temperature36.0–37.5 °CControlled normothermia (ESICM/NACCS 2024 consensus). Fever raises CMRO₂ and worsens the cascade. Do not cool below this — see the hypothermia trials.
Sodium135–145 mEq/L generallySome refractory-ICP protocols use permissive hypernatremia (145–155), but this rests on observational data, hypernatremia is itself associated with mortality, and COBI (JAMA 2021) found continuous 20% hypertonic saline targeting Na 150–155 for ≥48 h did not improve 6-month outcome. Use hyperosmolar therapy as boluses for ICP events, not as a continuous sodium goal.

CPP and osmolar gap

MAP (mmHg)
ICP (mmHg)
—
CPP = MAP − ICP. Target 60–70 mmHg.
Measured serum osmolality
Sodium (mEq/L)
BUN (mg/dL)
Glucose (mg/dL)
—
Calculated osm = 2×Na + BUN/2.8 + glucose/18. The gap (measured − calculated) tracks unexcreted mannitol.
Treat

The tiered ICP algorithm

🪜

SIBICC — escalate in order, de-escalate in reverse

The Seattle International Severe TBI Consensus Conference (Hawryluk et al., Intensive Care Medicine 2019 for the ICP algorithm and 2020 for the ICP+PbtO₂ version) produced a Delphi-consensus tiered approach from 42 international experts. It is Class III / consensus-based, not proven superior by RCT — but it is the closest thing to a shared mental model that this field has. The organizing principle: lower tiers have better risk profiles, so exhaust them before escalating, and when things improve, wean from the highest tier downwards.

The tiered approach to intracranial hypertension. Tier zero applies to every severe TBI patient whether or not the ICP is elevated — most of it costs nothing and is the part most often left undone.
0
Tier zero — everyone, all the time
Free, and constantly undone by routine care
▾

Head of bed 30° · head midline and cervical collar ties loosened (a tight collar obstructs jugular venous outflow and raises ICP measurably) · normothermia 36–37.5 °C · SpO₂ >94% · PaCO₂ 35–38 · adequate analgesia and sedation · treat seizures · sodium 135–145 · glucose 140–180 · head-up positioning maintained during transport and imaging.

Before escalating for a rising ICP, physically look at the patient: is the collar tight, is the head turned, is the patient bucking the ventilator, are they in pain, is there a distended bladder, is the EVD clamped or leveled wrong? A remarkable fraction of "refractory intracranial hypertension" is a positioning or sedation problem.
1
Tier one
Sedation, CSF drainage, hyperosmolar bolus
▾
  • Deepen analgesia and sedation — the cheapest way to cut CMRO₂ and abolish ICP spikes.
  • CSF drainage if an EVD is in place; consider converting a parenchymal monitor to an EVD specifically to gain the ability to drain.
  • Mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg IV bolus, or a hypertonic saline bolus (see the table below).
  • PaCO₂ to low-normal (35).
  • Anti-seizure prophylaxis for 1 week only; consider EEG monitoring if the exam and ICP do not match.
2
Tier two
Rescan, paralyse, test autoregulation
▾
  • Repeat the CT — the most important item in this tier. A new or expanded surgical lesion is the commonest reason tier-one therapy stops working.
  • Mild hypocapnia, PaCO₂ 32–35.
  • Neuromuscular blockade trial (cisatracurium) — abolishes coughing, shivering and ventilator dyssynchrony. A single bolus up to 4× ED95 caused no significant change in cerebral blood flow velocity, ICP, CPP, MAP or heart rate in brain-injured patients. Requires deep sedation and continuous EEG if prolonged.
  • MAP challenge to test autoregulation — raise the MAP by a defined increment and watch what the ICP does. If ICP falls, autoregulation is intact and raising CPP with vasopressors is rational; if ICP rises with MAP, it is pressure-passive and pushing CPP will make things worse.
  • Add a PbtO₂ monitor if not already placed.
3
Tier three — high risk, last resort
Craniectomy, barbiturates, rescue hyperventilation
▾
  • Secondary decompressive craniectomy — see the rescue section for the DECRA/RESCUEicp distinction, which is essential here.
  • Pentobarbital coma to burst suppression. Loading regimens described include 10 mg/kg IV over 30 min then 5 mg/kg every hour × 3 (~25 mg/kg cumulative), or 2.5 mg/kg every 15 min × 4 then 5 mg/kg/hr × 3 h; maintenance 1–3 mg/kg/hr, titrated on continuous EEG to roughly 2–5 bursts per minute. Requires ventilation, arterial line, central access and usually vasopressors — barbiturates cause myocardial depression and hypotension, and the resulting fall in MAP can cost you more CPP than the ICP reduction gains.
  • Mild hypothermia 35–36 °C is listed in the SIBICC tier, but note this is controlled cooling toward the low end of normothermia, not the 32–35 °C therapeutic hypothermia that failed in Eurotherm3235 and POLAR.
  • Rescue hyperventilation to PaCO₂ 30–32 — bridge only, ideally with PbtO₂ or jugular venous oximetry to detect the ischemia you may be causing.

Hyperosmolar therapy — the dosing

AgentDoseRepeatWhy / when to preferMonitor / ceiling
Mannitol 20–25%0.25–1 g/kg IV bolusEvery 4–6 h Osmotic gradient (reflection coefficient ~0.9) plus a rheologic effect — lowers blood viscosity, improving oxygen delivery, which triggers autoregulatory vasoconstriction and shrinks cerebral blood volume. Causes an osmotic diuresis — avoid or use very cautiously if hypovolemic or hypotensive, because the MAP you lose costs more CPP than the ICP you gain. Hold and reassess at serum osmolality ≥320 mOsm/kg. Follow osmolality and the osmolar gap 2–4× daily, plus renal function and volume status. Needs a Foley and free-water replacement.
Hypertonic saline 3%250 mL over 10–20 minCan be repeated as often as every 6 h; also runs as a continuous peripheral infusion (rates up to ~75 mL/h have an established peripheral safety profile) Reflection coefficient ~1.0 — the least able of the osmotic agents to cross an intact barrier, and it expands intravascular volume rather than depleting it. Preferred when the patient is hypovolemic or hypotensive — it supports MAP while lowering ICP. Follow sodium and chloride; hyperchloremic acidosis and renal injury with sustained use.
Hypertonic saline 23.4%30 mL over ~10–15 min via a CENTRAL lineAs an ICP crisis/herniation rescue Same mechanism, delivered as a small-volume, fast-acting bolus — the herniation drug. Central access is mandatory — extravasation causes tissue necrosis. Case series support administration over 2–5 minutes in a crisis, but 10–15 min is the conservative standard. Check sodium after.
Choosing between them is mostly a volume-status decision, not an efficacy one. Both lower ICP; neither has demonstrated consistent mortality or functional-outcome superiority. Hypotensive or hypovolemic patient → hypertonic saline. Volume-overloaded patient with good renal function → mannitol. Herniating right now with central access → 23.4%. Intermediate 5% and 7.5% concentrations are used in some institutions but standardized bolus dosing for them could not be verified for this build — follow your local protocol.
Support

Sedation & analgesia

💉

Dosing, and the trade-off against the neuro exam

DrugDoseWhy it works hereWatch for
Propofol~5–50 mcg/kg/min (≈0.3–3 mg/kg/hr) Rapid on/off, so the exam can be reassessed quickly; lowers CMRO₂ and therefore cerebral blood flow and volume. The workhorse in neurocritical care for exactly the offset reason. Hypotension — it will cost you CPP, and that matters more here than anywhere else. Propofol infusion syndrome risk rises with rates >4 mg/kg/hr sustained beyond 48 h (TBI is itself a described risk factor): watch for metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hypertriglyceridemia, arrhythmia. Count the lipid calories.
FentanylBolus and infusion titrated to pain and sedation goals Analgesia first — much apparent agitation is untreated pain, and pain drives ICP directly. Accumulates with prolonged infusion; chest-wall rigidity with rapid boluses; ileus. Blunts the exam.
KetamineBolus ~0.5–2 mg/kg; infusion ~5–40 mcg/kg/min (≈0.3–2.4 mg/kg/hr) Preserves blood pressure rather than dropping it, so it protects CPP — a genuine advantage in this population. Also analgesic and an NMDA antagonist. The "ketamine raises ICP" teaching is obsolete. It traces to 1970s case reports in patients with abnormal CSF pathways, none of whom had TBI. Contemporary meta-analysis across 101 adult and 55 paediatric patients found ICP did not rise in any included study, and it may fall. Ketamine is now a reasonable — sometimes preferred — induction and sedation agent in TBI.
Dexmedetomidine0.2–0.7 mcg/kg/hr (usually skip the 0.5–0.8 mcg/kg load to avoid hypotension) α2 agonist — arousable sedation without respiratory depression, so the neuro exam survives. Useful in weaning and in agitation. Bradycardia and hypotension. Not a sufficient sole agent for deep sedation or for ICP control.
Midazolam~0.05 mg/kg IV initially; 0.01–0.05 mg/kg/hr Anticonvulsant and amnestic; useful when propofol cannot be tolerated hemodynamically. Accumulates badly in organ dysfunction, clouding the exam for days. Benzodiazepine exposure is associated with delirium and impaired cognitive recovery — use the least you can.
CisatracuriumReported infusion range ~0.75–4.5 mcg/kg/min (institution-variable) Abolishes coughing, shivering and dyssynchrony — all potent ICP amplifiers. Organ-independent Hofmann elimination, so it is predictable in renal and hepatic failure. Only after sedation and analgesia are already adequate — a paralysed, under-sedated patient is a catastrophe. Removes the neuro exam entirely, so pair with continuous EEG. Critical illness myopathy with prolonged use.
Every sedative here buys ICP control by spending your ability to examine the patient. That trade is worth making — but it means the ICP number, the pupils and the imaging become your exam, and it raises the threshold for noticing a new lesion. This is the practical argument for a daily plan that specifies when sedation will be lightened, and for a low threshold to rescan when it cannot be.
Support

Pressors & hemodynamics

📊

Which drip, why, and the dose

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHemodynamic effectWhen to pick it in TBI
NorepinephrinePotent α1, modest β1~0.01–3 mcg/kg/min, start low and titrate↑ SVR with some inotropy; predictable, linear responseFirst line in most neuro-ICU protocols — chosen for titratability and predictability rather than proven outcome superiority. Animal data suggest it produces higher PbtO₂ than phenylephrine at similar CBF.
PhenylephrinePure α1, no β activity~0.1–0.5 mcg/kg/min (≈40–180 mcg/min)↑ SVR with reflex bradycardia; no inotropyUseful when tachyarrhythmia limits norepinephrine. One severe-TBI study found phenylephrine achieved 12 mmHg higher CPP than norepinephrine over the first 3 hours — though injured-brain models show higher cerebral glycerol and lactate/pyruvate ratios with it, a concerning metabolic signal.
VasopressinV1 receptor, catecholamine-independentFixed 0.01–0.04 units/min↑ SVR without adrenergic stimulationAdjunct to spare catecholamine dose, not a first-line agent. Caution: promotes free-water retention in a population already prone to SIADH — follow sodium closely.
Epinephrineβ1, β2, α1~0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑ CO and SVRSecond or third line. Tachyarrhythmia and lactate elevation confound your monitoring.
DopamineDose-dependent: D1 <3 · β1 3–10 · α1 >10 mcg/kg/minUp to 20 mcg/kg/minVariable by doseLargely abandoned — arrhythmia risk with no advantage. Not preferred in TBI.
You are not treating blood pressure — you are buying CPP = MAP − ICP. That means there are always two levers, and the ICP lever is usually the better one: lowering ICP by 10 mmHg gains exactly as much CPP as raising MAP by 10, without the pressor. Reach for the vasopressor when ICP is already being addressed, when the MAP challenge showed autoregulation is intact, and remember not to push CPP past 70 — the aggressive-CPP strategy causes ARDS without improving the brain.
Level the arterial line transducer at the tragus (the external auditory meatus, approximating the foramen of Monro) rather than the phlebostatic axis when you are calculating CPP. Leveling at the heart in a head-up patient overestimates cerebral MAP by roughly 2 mmHg per 2.5 cm of height difference — enough to make a CPP of 55 read as 65.
Airway

Ventilation

🌬️

Lung-protective settings in a brain-protective patient

Mode
AC/VC
volume control, fully controlled early
Tidal volume
6–8 mL/kg
predicted body weight
PEEP
5–8 to start
individualize with ICP watched
PaCO₂
35–38
the number that matters most
SpO₂ / PaO₂
>94% / >100
avoid hypoxia and extreme hyperoxia
Plateau pressure
<30 cmH₂O
standard lung protection

Lung-protective ventilation is safe in brain injury. The old fear that low tidal volumes and PEEP would raise ICP has not held up: moderate PEEP (studied to 10–15 cmH₂O in some protocols, and 5 vs 12 cmH₂O head-to-head) did not elevate ICP. Individualize PEEP with ICP monitored rather than reflexively withholding it — the hypoxemia and hypercapnia of an under-supported lung are far more damaging to the brain than the PEEP would have been.

Prophylactic hyperventilation is a BTF Level IIB "do not." Prolonged hyperventilation to PaCO₂ ≤25 mmHg is not recommended at all, and hyperventilation should be avoided entirely in the first 24 hours, when cerebral blood flow is often already critically low — you would be adding CO₂-mediated vasoconstriction on top of existing hypoperfusion. Rescue hyperventilation to 30–32 mmHg is a bridge to definitive treatment measured in minutes, not a management strategy.
Tracheostomy by about day 7 in patients expected to need prolonged ventilation. Early tracheostomy consistently shortens ventilator days and ICU stay (9.6 vs 18.7 ventilator days, and 10.9 vs 21.0 ICU days in one trauma cohort) but has not shown a consistent mortality benefit — say that plainly to families rather than implying it improves survival.
Rescue

Surgery & rescue therapies

⚙️

What the operating room can and cannot fix

Evacuation thresholds

LesionOperateNon-operative management acceptable
Epidural hematoma>30 cm³ — evacuate regardless of GCS. A comatose patient (GCS <9) with an EDH and anisocoria needs emergent evacuation.<30 cm³ and <15 mm thick and <5 mm midline shift, in a patient with GCS >8 and no focal deficit — with serial CT and close neurologic observation at a neurosurgical centre.
Acute subdural hematomaThickness >10 mm OR midline shift >5 mm — evacuate regardless of GCS.Below both thresholds with a stable exam, monitored closely.

Brain Trauma Foundation surgical management guidelines. These figures date from the 2006 surgical guidelines, which remain the standard reference.

An epidural hematoma is the most reversible lesion in all of TBI — it is extra-axial arterial blood compressing an otherwise healthy brain. Evacuated in time, outcomes are excellent. That is the reason a patient with an EDH and a lucid interval is the classic "do not send home" teaching case, and also why the Rotterdam score paradoxically gives a point for the absence of an EDH.

Decompressive craniectomy — why two landmark trials disagree

DECRA (NEJM 2011)RESCUEicp (NEJM 2016)
Populationn=155. Diffuse severe TBI, early — ICP >20 mmHg within the first 72 h, refractory to first-tier therapyn=408, ages 10–65. Late — ICP >25 mmHg for 1–12 h despite tier 1–2 management
OperationBifrontotemporoparietal craniectomyUnilateral frontotemporoparietal or bifrontal
ResultICP fell (14.4 vs 19.1 mmHg, p<0.001) and ICU/ventilator days shortened, but unfavourable GOS-E was worse: 70% vs 51% (OR 2.21, 95% CI 1.14–4.26, p=0.02). Mortality unchanged (19% vs 18%).Mortality fell: 26.9% vs 48.9% at 6 months. But vegetative state was higher (8.5% vs 2.1%) and lower severe disability higher (21.9% vs 14.4%) — survivors were shifted into more disabled categories.
ReadingThey are not contradictory — they tested different interventions at different points in the disease. Early prophylactic-style craniectomy for moderate intracranial hypertension trades function for a number. Late craniectomy as genuine salvage for refractory hypertension trades mortality for morbidity — it converts deaths into survivors, some of whom are severely disabled. That is a real choice a family can be asked about; it is not a technical decision.
BTF 2020 Decompressive Craniectomy Update formalized exactly this split: secondary DC for late refractory intracranial hypertension is recommended to improve mortality and favourable outcomes (Level IIA); secondary DC for early refractory elevation is not recommended (Level IIA); and when it is done, a large frontotemporoparietal craniectomy (≥12 × 15 cm or ≥15 cm diameter) is recommended over a small one (Level IIA) — too small a flap causes venous infarction at the bone edges.

RESCUE-ASDH (NEJM 2023, n=450) asked a different question: when you evacuate an acute subdural, do you put the bone flap back (craniotomy) or leave it out (primary craniectomy)? At 12 months, death was 30.2% vs 32.2% and the GOS-E distribution was not significantly different (common OR 0.85, 95% CI 0.60–1.18). The trade-off is in complications: more reoperation with craniotomy (14.6% vs 6.9%), more wound complications with craniectomy (12.2% vs 3.9%). Individualize.

Things that lower ICP and do not help

Hypothermia — three negative RCTs. Eurotherm3235 (NEJM 2015; 32–35 °C for ICP >20 refractory to tier 1) was stopped early for safety with a signal of worse outcomes. POLAR (JAMA 2018, n=511; early prophylactic cooling) found favourable 6-month outcome in 48.8% vs 49.1% — no difference. NABIS:H II (Lancet Neurology 2011; cooling to 33 °C within 2.5 h) was also negative. Hypothermia reliably lowers ICP and reliably fails to help. Controlled normothermia is the standard, not cooling.
Corticosteroids — do not give them. CRASH-1 (n=10,008): 6-month mortality 25.7% vs 22.3%, RR 1.15 (95% CI 1.07–1.24), p=0.0001; the trial was stopped early. This is one of the very few Level I "never do this" recommendations in TBI. Steroids for the vasogenic edema of a brain tumour are correct; the identical reasoning applied to trauma kills people.

Barbiturate coma lowers ICP reliably but has never been shown to improve outcome when used prophylactically (BTF rates the evidence low quality). It is a tier-three salvage option, dosed as above, and it costs you the exam, the blood pressure, and often several days of drug clearance before prognostication is even possible.

Neuroprotective drugs have a long graveyard worth knowing about: progesterone failed in two simultaneous phase 3 trials (PROTECT III and SYNAPSE, both NEJM 2014) despite outstanding preclinical data, and erythropoietin failed in both Robertson's JAMA 2014 trial and EPO-TBI. There is currently no drug that reverses the secondary injury cascade — which is precisely why the unglamorous physiologic targets in tier zero carry the outcome.

Downgrade

Downgrade & prognosis

⬇️

Stepping down, and talking about the future

Ready to downgrade when all of: neurologic exam stable or improving · ICP controlled for ~24 hours without escalating therapy, and monitor removed or ready to come out · no new lesion on the most recent imaging · off vasopressors and hemodynamically stable · airway secure — extubated, or tracheostomy with manageable secretions · no active seizures · sodium and glucose stable within target on a maintainable regimen.
Not yet if: therapy was escalated for ICP control within the last 24 hours · coagulopathy is uncorrected · a repeat CT is pending after a new deficit · paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity episodes are still occurring and needing intervention · hyperosmolar boluses are still being given · the patient is on a pentobarbital wean and has not cleared the drug · secretions or airway protection remain marginal.

No single numbered guideline defines TBI ICU downgrade criteria — these synthesize standard neurocritical care de-escalation practice. Follow your unit's protocol where one exists.

Prognostication

Two validated models, both computed at source rather than reimplemented here:

  • IMPACT — core: age, motor score, pupillary reactivity. Extended adds CT classification and secondary insults (hypoxia, hypotension). Lab adds glucose and hemoglobin. Predicts 6-month mortality and unfavourable outcome. Compute on MDCalc.
  • CRASH — basic: country income setting, GCS, pupillary reactivity, major extracranial injury. CT model adds petechial hemorrhage, obliterated basal cisterns, subarachnoid blood, midline shift, non-evacuated hematoma. Predicts 14-day mortality and 6-month unfavourable outcome. Compute at LSHTM.
The self-fulfilling prophecy. These models predict outcomes in populations that included patients in whom life-sustaining therapy was withdrawn because the prognosis looked poor. Institutional "withdrawal culture" independently predicts withdrawal decisions irrespective of clinical severity — meaning an early pessimistic prediction can become the cause of the outcome it forecast. Meaningful recovery after TBI continues for 1–2 years. Avoid definitive prognostication and irreversible decisions in the first 72 hours unless the injury is unequivocally unsurvivable, present prognostic estimates to families as population probabilities rather than individual verdicts, and say out loud that the number came from a model.

Brain death determination

Per the 2023 AAN/AAP/CNS/SCCM consensus practice guideline, which unified the previous adult and paediatric documents:

  • Prerequisites: a known, irreversible, catastrophic brain injury of established cause · normothermia (core temperature generally ≥36 °C) · adequate blood pressure · and exclusion of every confounder — sedative and paralytic effect (accounting for hepatic and renal clearance, with drug levels or adequate half-life waiting), severe electrolyte, acid–base or endocrine derangement, and anything that could mimic the examination.
  • Examination: coma with no response to noxious stimulus, and complete absence of brainstem reflexes — pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic and oculovestibular (cold caloric), gag and cough.
  • Apnea test: a formal protocol, with defined modifications for patients on ECMO. The long-standing target incorporated into the guideline is a PaCO₂ rise of ≥20 mmHg above baseline and to an absolute value ≥60 mmHg with no respiratory effort.
  • Ancillary testing (cerebral blood flow study or EEG) when the examination or apnea test cannot be completed safely.
  • The 2023 document also addresses consent for testing, evaluation during pregnancy, preservation of neuroendocrine function, and primary posterior fossa injury.

Always follow your institution's brain death policy and local law, which govern the number of examiners and observation intervals.

Pearls

Practice-changing pearls

💡

Seventeen things that change what you do

  1. Steroids kill in TBI. CRASH-1, n=10,008: 6-month mortality 25.7% vs 22.3%, RR 1.15 (95% CI 1.07–1.24), p=0.0001. One of the only Level I "never" recommendations in the field.
  2. The blood pressure floor is age-stratified and not monotonic. SBP ≥110 mmHg if 15–49 or over 70; ≥100 mmHg if 50–69. Both the youngest and the oldest need the higher floor.
  3. Early and late decompressive craniectomy are different operations. DECRA (early, ICP >20 within 72 h) worsened function; RESCUEicp (late, ICP >25 refractory to tiers 1–2) cut mortality nearly in half but produced more severely disabled survivors. The 2020 BTF update recommends against the first and for the second.
  4. The ketamine–ICP myth is dead. Meta-analysis across 101 adult and 55 paediatric patients found ICP did not rise in any included study. Ketamine's blood-pressure support is an advantage when you are defending CPP.
  5. Do not transfuse platelets for antiplatelet-associated intracranial hemorrhage. PATCH: adjusted OR 2.05 (95% CI 1.18–3.56) for death or dependence with transfusion.
  6. TXA helps early, and helps the patients with the most left to lose. CRASH-3 was null overall (18.5% vs 19.8%) but significant in the GCS 9–15 subgroup (5.8% vs 7.5%, RR 0.78). Give it within 3 hours or not at all.
  7. Three hypothermia RCTs, three failures. Eurotherm3235 (stopped early for harm), POLAR (48.8% vs 49.1%) and NABIS:H II. Lowering ICP is not the same as helping the patient — the single most important idea in TBI.
  8. Liberal transfusion does not help. HEMOTION found no significant benefit to a Hgb 10 target, and Robertson 2014 found more thromboembolic events with it. Transfuse at ~7 g/dL.
  9. ICP monitoring is a tool, not a religion. BEST-TRIP showed protocolized imaging- and exam-driven care matched monitor-driven care (HR 1.10). The algorithm and the diligence carry the outcome.
  10. Andexanet alfa is not a free lunch. ANNEXA-I: hemostatic efficacy 67.0% vs 53.1%, but thrombotic events 10.3% vs 5.6% including ischemic stroke.
  11. Seven days of seizure prophylaxis, then stop. Temkin 1990 (3.6% vs 14.2% early seizures) is the entire evidence base and showed no benefit for late seizures. Write the stop date in the orders.
  12. Levetiracetam and phenytoin are equally effective, not equally tolerated. Early-seizure RR 1.10 (95% CI 0.64–1.88) with fewer adverse reactions on levetiracetam — the reason it displaced phenytoin.
  13. SIADH and cerebral salt wasting look identical on labs and need opposite treatment. Volume status is the only reliable discriminator, and fluid-restricting a volume-depleted patient drops their cerebral perfusion pressure.
  14. Amantadine speeds the pace of recovery; it is not a cure. Giacino's NEJM 2012 benefit was a rate effect during active treatment that attenuated on stopping.
  15. Screen the pituitary at 3 months. About 56% of moderate–severe TBI survivors have at least one impaired axis — and it presents as fatigue and low mood that get blamed on the brain injury.
  16. Early tracheostomy buys ICU days, not survival. Consistently fewer ventilator and ICU days, no consistent mortality benefit. Say that to families accurately.
  17. Beware the self-fulfilling prophecy. Institutional withdrawal culture independently predicts withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy irrespective of severity, and recovery continues for 1–2 years. Do not make irreversible decisions in the first 72 hours on the strength of a model.

Accuracy notes — where this guide is deliberately less precise

Read this before quoting a number from here Every figure above traces to a cited source. The following could not be verified to a primary source during this build and are presented with that limitation stated in place, rather than dropped or guessed:
  • BIG millimetre thresholds. Only the categorical tiers and their management were confirmed; the per-lesion mm cutoffs come from secondary sources. Use your institution's adopted BIG/mBIG protocol.
  • Amsterdam 2023 verbatim wording of the concussion definition and the return-to-sport step titles — the BJSM primary text is paywalled. The 6-step structure is concordant across CDC HEADS UP, AAP and World Rugby summaries.
  • Helsinki CT score full point table — incomplete, so it is referenced but not reimplemented. IMPACT and CRASH are linked out for the same reason: their arithmetic could not be verified point-by-point.
  • Levetiracetam prophylaxis loading dose — institutional protocols vary from 500 mg to weight-based 20–60 mg/kg. The 20 mg/kg load with 1,000 mg q12h maintenance is the commonly described protocol, not a universal standard.
  • Trazodone, nortriptyline and methylphenidate dosing in TBI — no TBI-specific ladder could be sourced to a primary pharmacology reference. Dose from a formal drug reference.
  • 5% and 7.5% hypertonic saline bolus dosing — institution-variable; only 3% and 23.4% have consistently described regimens.
  • ICU downgrade criteria — no single numbered guideline exists; the criteria given synthesize standard neurocritical care practice.
  • BOOST-3 final results were not confirmed as published at build time — no result numbers are quoted for it here.
  • Brain death apnea-test thresholds (PaCO₂ rise ≥20 mmHg and ≥60 mmHg absolute) reflect the long-standing standard carried into the 2023 guideline; the full guideline text could not be read verbatim. Follow your institutional policy.
  • Driving restrictions after post-traumatic seizure are jurisdiction-specific. The commonly cited 6-month seizure-free interval is not universal — check the local DMV rule.
